verses.translation_literal: Of David. A psalm. To YHWH [belongs] the earth and its fullness, the world and the dwellers in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David, sung from the lips of a people who stand with their faces up. The earth belongs to the LORD, the whole of it, and everything that fills it, to its brim. The wide world is his, and every soul that breathes upon it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a claim of ownership, and the Hebrew puts the owner first: "To YHWH, the earth." Nothing in the line is a wish or a hope; it is the deed to the land read out in a crowd, and it is meant to unsettle every other claim on it. In a world where each people had a god tied to its own hills and each king held his land by that god, a psalm that gave the whole earth to one deity was a statement against Baal and every other local master.

The KJV "The earth is the Lord's" supplies a verb Hebrew leaves out, and "fulness thereof" is archaic for the plain noun "what fills it": the full contents of the earth, its creatures and its crops and its peoples. Tradition spoke of the land of Israel and the other lands (Rashi), but the Hebrew sets two words side by side, "earth" and "world" (erets and tevel), with tevel the inhabited, farmed part, and the claim reaches both. The superscription "of David" gives the lamed of authorship or attribution, the same preposition that opens the line a moment later ("to YHWH") for possession.

philological_notes.note: A poetic word for the inhabited world, the settled land, as against erets, the earth as a whole. The pair of words sets 'the land and all it holds' beside 'the world and those who dwell in it'.
'And its fullness', from the root 'to be full': what fills the earth, its contents. Metzudat David reads it as all the things the earth is full of.

verses.translation_literal: For he, upon seas, founded it, and upon rivers he established it.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it was he who laid its footings in the seas and set it firm upon the rivers. The deep ran beneath it, and he made it stand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the claim in verse 1 is given in a picture of the world that every hearer shared: the dry land is a platform raised over the waters of the deep, with the seas below and the rivers running under it. A people who watched the Mediterranean and the Jordan did not need this explained. "For he" puts weight on the pronoun: he, and no one else, did this. The Hebrew keeps the two verbs apart, "founded" and "established", and the two water-words apart, "seas" and "rivers" (yammim and neharot), as a parallel pair and not a repetition.

The KJV "floods" for neharot hides the plain word "rivers". Ancient readers also heard a taunt: the sea and the rivers were, in the neighbouring religions, divine powers (Yam, and Nahar in the Ugaritic texts), and here they are only the ground under the feet of YHWH's earth. Rashi and Radak read the waters as the seas and rivers around the land of Israel, but the plain sense is the cosmic one.

philological_notes.note: 'He founded it': to lay a foundation. Paired with yekhonenah, 'he established it', from the root 'to be firm', so the line says 'laid down and made firm'.
'Rivers'; the KJV 'floods' loses the plain word. The pairing 'sea and river' recalls the divine names Yam and Nahar of Ugaritic poetry, which I mention as my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: Who will go up in the mountain of YHWH, and who will stand in the place of his holiness?
verses.translation_dramatic: And who may climb the mountain of the LORD? Who may stand, and keep standing, in the place that is his and set apart?
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. After a verse of cosmic grandeur the voice drops to a question, and the question is a hard one: if the whole earth belongs to him, who is allowed near? This is the voice of a pilgrim at the foot of the hill, or of a priest at the gate asking the entrance liturgy, and the question is meant to be answered by the group (as it is in the next verse). It belongs to a known form, the "entrance torah" (compare Psalm 15 and Isaiah 33:14-16).

Two things the KJV flattens. "Hill" for har: the word is "mountain", the temple mount, and the climb is a real one. And "stand" (yaqum) is not just standing; it is to rise and hold one's place, to keep a position in his presence. "His holy place" is literally "the place of his holiness", a phrase that makes the place itself the gift of that holiness. The tradition (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David) reads the mountain as the temple mount.

philological_notes.note: 'Go up', the usual verb of pilgrimage: one goes up to the temple. The cohortative colour is not in the form; it is a plain imperfect asking who 'will' or 'may'.
'Rise, stand': not only to be standing but to take a stand and hold it, here in the sacred place.

verses.translation_literal: Clean of hands and pure of heart, who has not lifted up my self to falsehood, and has not sworn to deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: The one whose hands are clean and whose heart is clear, who has not lifted his soul toward what is empty, and has never sworn an oath to deceive.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer comes without a pause, and it is a list of four things in the order of a whole life: hands, heart, the self, the tongue. Hands are what a person does; "heart" (levav) is what the person means; the nefesh is the person's appetite and longing; and the oath is the person's word. A man who passes all four is whole, and the test is moral, not ritual: no washing, no sacrifice, no pedigree is named.

Three places where the English softens. "Clean hands" is literally "clean of palms" (kappayim), the palms being the part of a person that takes and gives; a clean palm has not taken what is not its own. "Lifted up his soul unto vanity" is the KJV's reading; shav' means falsehood, emptiness, the worthless and the lie, and "vanity" has drifted in English towards vain pride. And the form in the Hebrew text is "my" nefesh (the written text has "his"). Rashi and Radak hear God speaking here, with the same idiom as "the Lord has sworn by his nefesh" (Jer 51:14, Amos 6:8): not to swear falsely by God's name. The Targum already reads it as swearing falsely. "Deceit" (mirmah) is the same word used of Jacob's trick on Isaac and of Laban's on Jacob, a word with a cunning edge to it.

philological_notes.note: Qere 'my self' (nefesh), the written text (Ketiv) has 'his'. 'To lift up the nefesh' is to long for something or set one's desire on it (Ps 25:1); with the Qere reading, God speaks and the verb refers to his name. nefesh covers life, self, throat and appetite, so the English 'soul' is only one part of it.
Falsehood, emptiness, what is worthless. It is the word of the third commandment ('do not lift up the name of YHWH your God to shav'), which is why the tradition reads this as swearing falsely.
'Palms, hands': the hands as the part that takes and gives; 'clean of palms' means free of what was taken wrongly.

verses.translation_literal: He will lift up a blessing from with YHWH, and righteousness from the God of his salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: That one will lift a blessing from the LORD's own hand, and a verdict of right from the God who saves him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reward answers the oath-breaker's crime in verse 4. There the one who is fit for the mountain "did not lift up" his longing to what is empty; here the same verb, nasa', is used for what he lifts from God: a blessing. Ibn Ezra sets the two lines side by side, so the echo is the point, and an actor should let the word come back with the same weight. The man who would not lift up falsehood lifts up a gift.

The tradition hears the verb as "take" or "receive". Radak glosses it "take" and compares Naaman's plea to Elisha, "take, please, a blessing from your servant" (2 Kings 5:15), where "blessing" is a present handed over; Meiri glosses it "receive", and the Targum renders "he will receive". So the KJV "shall receive" is a sound reading of the sense, and it is the same reading the old Jewish translators made; what it cannot show in English is that the Hebrew uses the very verb of verse 4. "Blessing" here is not a warm feeling but a gift of life and standing, and tsedaqah, "righteousness", is not a private virtue but a verdict in the person's favour, the vindication a judge grants. The preposition me'et, "from with", puts the gift in God's own hand. "God of his salvation" is the Hebrew's plain phrase for the God who rescues him; Radak says it means he saves him from every trouble.

philological_notes.note: 'He will lift up': the same verb as 'has not lifted up' in verse 4, so the blessing answers the oath. Radak glosses it 'take' and compares 2 Kings 5:15; Meiri glosses 'receive'; the Targum has 'he will receive'.

'Righteousness': here as the verdict or vindication God gives to the one who comes in right standing, set beside 'blessing'. Malbim hears in it a grace that does not look at a person's preparation or deeds.

verses.translation_literal: This [is] the generation of those who seek him, those who seek your face, Jacob. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is the kind of people who seek him: those who seek your face. This is Jacob. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The congregation answers its own question. "Generation" (dor) here is a kind of people, a type and not only an age: these are the ones who do come up. Then the voice turns without warning from "him" to "your face", and the poet speaks to God directly (Radak: the poet speaks toward God). That swerve from third person to second is the heart of the verse, and the actor should turn his body with it.

"Jacob" stands bare, and the traditional readers take it as the name of the seekers: those who seek your face are Jacob, the whole of Israel, whom Scripture often calls by the patriarch's name, as in "fear not, my servant Jacob" (Jer 30:10, cited by Radak). Ibn Ezra reads it as "the seed of Jacob", Meiri as the whole community of Israel, and Metzudat David the same. The KJV and Webster have "O Jacob", a vocative, as though God or the people were being addressed in a new voice; that is a different reading and sits oddly after "your face", which is said to God. The ASV "even Jacob" and YLT's "O Jacob" fall on either side; the BBE "God of Jacob" adds words the Hebrew lacks, and Ibn Ezra says there is no need for them. Malbim has a further idea: the whole generation stands at the rank of Jacob, who saw the ladder that joins earth to heaven. "Seek the face" is the language of coming into a king's presence. Selah is a mark of uncertain sense; I leave it as it is.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who seek him'. The written text (Ketiv) has a singular suffix, the reading (Qere) the plural; Radak says the written singular matches the collective 'generation' and the read plural matches the individuals who make it up.

'Jacob' as the name of the seekers, meaning all his descendants. Radak takes it so, citing Jeremiah 30:10, and says there is no need to add 'seed' as other commentators do; Ibn Ezra reads 'the seed of Jacob'; Meiri 'the whole of Israel'. The KJV 'O Jacob' is a vocative reading.
A musical or liturgical mark of uncertain meaning. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'truly'; Meiri as 'forever'. Radak says he explained it at Psalm 3 and will not repeat it.

verses.translation_literal: Lift up, gates, your heads, and be lifted up, doors of antiquity, so that the king of the glory may come in.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lift your heads, you gates! Rise, you ancient doors, rise up, and let the King of glory come in!
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene changes: the people are now at the gates of the sanctuary, and the speaker commands the gates themselves, as if they were living guards. "Lift up your heads" is a drama of height: the lintels are the heads of the gates, and the gates are told to stand taller than they are, to make room for one who is greater than any door was built for. The ancient picture is of a procession, perhaps the ark brought into the city of David (2 Sam 6) or into Solomon's temple; tradition (Rashi, Radak) tells how the gates stuck together until Solomon prayed. The text itself says none of this.

The verb "lift up" is the third use of the root nasa' in the psalm (verses 4 and 5 used it for the oath and the blessing), and the second verb is passive-reflexive, "be lifted". "Everlasting doors" in the KJV is a fair reading of the Hebrew pitkhe olam, 'doors of antiquity': it can mean long-standing or lasting. Radak's point, that the ark had moved from place to place and now had a permanent house, explains why the doors can be called olam. The phrase "the King of glory" (melekh hakkavod) is with the article: the King, the Glory.

philological_notes.note: 'Lift up', imperative, the same root as 'lifted up' in verses 4 and 5; the verb comes back with a new sense, to raise something that blocks the way.

'Doors of olam': ancient, or lasting. Radak and Metzudat David read 'permanent': the sanctuary that no longer moves. Radak adds that sha'ar is the gate with its threshold and posts, and petakh the doors.
'The King of glory': kavod is weight and honour, the glory that shows God's presence. Radak ties it to the ark and the glory that dwelt between the cherubim.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] this king of the glory? YHWH, strong and mighty, YHWH, mighty of battle.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty! The LORD, mighty in battle!
verses.directors_commentary:
The gates answer, or the people speak for them: "Who is he, this King of glory?" It is a challenge and a ritual question: a gatekeeper does not open to a name he does not know. The answer is the name and then two titles of war. The words are blunt: "strong" (izzuz) and "mighty" (gibbor), the language of a soldier, and then the full phrase "mighty of battle". This is a warrior-king returning, and the doors are asked to open to a general.

The KJV "mighty in battle" is accurate enough; the Hebrew has a construct, "hero of war". The plain picture is of the ark going out with the army (Radak, Meiri), and the claim to be "king of glory" is set against the claims of every other god who ruled by war. Notice that the second title repeats the divine name: YHWH, YHWH, as a drumbeat.

philological_notes.note: 'Strong': from the root of 'strength', with the doubled consonant giving an intensive sense. Metzudat Zion ties it to oz, strength.
'Hero of battle', the standard title for a champion; here it is given to YHWH. Radak and Meiri connect it to the ark going out to war.

verses.translation_literal: Lift up, gates, your heads, and lift up [your heads], doors of antiquity, so that the king of the glory may come in.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lift your heads, you gates! Lift them, you ancient doors, lift them high, and let the King of glory come in!
verses.directors_commentary:
The command comes again, louder, as a second wave. Only one thing changes in the words: in verse 7 the doors were told "be lifted up" (a passive form, as though something outside raised them); now they are told "lift up", the plain active. I read that as the doors taking the lifting on themselves, a gate that after the first shove opens of its own will. The commentators speak instead of repetition (Radak: the doubling is the habit of the language, one idea in different words), so the reading of the verb is mine.

The Hebrew is shorter than it looks: the doors are told "and lift up" with no object, and the object is carried over from the first colon. Ibn Ezra paraphrases it as "and lift up, doors of antiquity, your heads", and Radak adds that the one "your heads" does duty for two. I have put it in brackets in the literal layer. The KJV "even lift them up" and ASV "yea, lift them up" supply "them" to say the same, and are fair. Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra hear two houses in the doubling, the first temple and the future one, because the glory did not rest in the second; that is their reading and not the plain sense. The Targum has a surprise: here the gates are the gates of the Garden of Eden, not of the temple, which shows how freely the tradition heard the verse.

philological_notes.note: 'And lift up', qal imperative, in place of the niphal 'be lifted up' of verse 7. The commentators call the doubling a repetition of the idea (kefel); that the doors move from being lifted to lifting is my own reading of the form.
'Your heads', carried over from the first colon to the second. Ibn Ezra writes it out: 'and lift up, doors of antiquity, your heads'; Radak says the one word stands for two, as the language does.

verses.translation_literal: Who, he, [is] this king of the glory? YHWH of hosts, he [is] the king of the glory. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who then is he, this King of glory? The LORD of hosts! He, he is the King of glory. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The question returns, sharper by one word: "Who, he, this king of glory?" The extra "he" (hu') points a finger at the one waiting at the gate. The answer is no longer the warrior of verse 8 but a new title, "YHWH of hosts" (tseva'ot), the commander of the armies, of heaven and of earth. The KJV "Lord of hosts" keeps the name; "hosts" means armies, the whole array of the heavens and of Israel's forces (Ibn Ezra reads the host of heaven).

The last line is the loudest of the psalm: "he, he is the King of glory", and with its repetition of the pronoun it ends on the claim that opened the psalm, ownership, now of the doors and the city. Radak and Meiri observe that "mighty in battle" has dropped away, because the ark is now at rest; that reading is theirs, not the text's.

philological_notes.note: 'YHWH of hosts': the commander of armies. Ibn Ezra reads it as the host of heaven, against the Gaon's reading of Israel's army; Radak takes it as the armies of Israel coming to the house.
A mark of uncertain meaning, closing the psalm. Metzudat David reads 'forever'.
